source_document.body:
The most shocking thing about the recent investors day presentation held by Expeditors International is that it was taking place at all.
Daniel Wall, the president and CEO of the asset-light freight forwarder–among several other services–conceded at the start of the November 18 investors day event that “if you know me well, you know I probably came here kicking and screaming a little bit.”
Expeditors (NYSE: EXPD) does not have an earnings call with analysts after it releases its quarterly earnings. Wall said the investors day was the first Expeditors had held in 11 years.
Unlike other company investor days, which are usually closed-door and open just to analysts who follow the company, Expeditors’ was broadcast and anybody could have signed up for it if they were aware of its existence.
“We have to engage better with the investment community,” Wall said, according to a transcript of the event. “And today is an attempt to do that. We’re going to give you some insights into some things that we don’t normally share.”
CFO with the big reveal
Most of the revelations about Expeditors’ business that had not been released previously came from Dave Hackett, the company’s CFO. He spoke of “two things that we’ve never disclosed.”
The first, which he described as “a little bit tactical but strategic,” was the role of Expeditor’s business tied to technology and by extension, AI.
Hackett revealed that 35% of Expeditors’ gross revenue is coming from its technology vertical. That is by far the largest; healthcare is second at 14%.
The pre-AI comparison, Hackett said, is that technology was about 28% of the company’s gross revenue in 2019.
“So is a lot of that AI?” Hackett said. “Yes. Is AI driving our results? Absolutely.”
Expeditors, Hackett said, is “heavily concentrated in the capex supercycle of the century. So that is a good thing and we’re performing very well.”
Business with hyperscalers was cited by Expeditors in its most recent quarterly earnings as a key driver of profitability.
The other verticals and their share of gross revenue disclosed by Hackett were retail, 13%; automotive, 12%; industrial, 6%; and aviation, 4%, leaving 14% to 15% for all other markets.
What’s in the customs brokerage operations?
The second big numerical reveal, which Hackett referred to as “more strategic,” was the breakdown in revenues for its customs brokerage segment.
Expeditors’ quarterly earnings report separate revenue figures for airfreight services, ocean freight and ocean services, and customs brokerage and other services. In the most recent quarterly earnings, airfreight was approximately 37.6% of revenues, ocean was about 26.8% with customs brokerage the balance at a little over 35%.
Hackett said that customs brokerage number can approach 50%, depending on the performance of the other two segments.
But within that segment, Hackett said, “A lot of investors and analysts think it’s all customs brokerage. It is not.”
The chart revealed by Hackett showed that customs brokerage revenues were 47% of the segment that carries that name in the quarterly earnings.
Its Transcon operations, which services the over-the-ground industry, is 37% of the segments’ revenue. In its most recent 10-K filing, Expeditors said Transcon “consists of intra-continental ground transportation, including time-definite less-than-truck and full-truck solutions.”
The remaining 16% of the segment is from warehousing & distribution. That Expeditors’ 10-K said its warehousing operations offer services such as inventory management and “are generally offered globally in multi-client facilities so that customers may benefit from cost savings related to shared space, labor, equipment, and other efficiencies.”
Hackett added he would not discuss the profitability of the sectors. There also was not a timeframe disclosed for those figures.
(An expanded area for Expeditors was recently announced: space travel. )
TD Securities raises its rating
The transportation research team at TD Securities led by Jason Seidl liked what they heard enough that they upgraded their rating to Hold from Sell within days after the investors meeting.
In its report, TD Securities noted that the discussion by Expeditors’ management about the use of AI in the company differed from what is heard from the leaders of C.H. Robinson (NASDAQ: CHRW). While the two companies are not head-to-head competitors in many businesses, they both are asset-light entities whose value proposition is to take responsibility for moving freight from point A to point B away from their customers and shifting it on to their own expert staff.
C.H. Robinson has seen a sharp reduction in headcount as it promotes its use of lean AI. But as TD Securities noted, the message from Expeditors was different.
“EXPD spent a significant portion of the day highlighting their employees, tenure and retention,” the TD report said. “EXPD does not plan to roll out a significant automation effort that will drive SG&A leverage but instead take a methodical approach to driving productivity and wallet share gains.”
It was noted by at least one analyst following the $EXPD investors day call that it is pushing AI as an efficiency tool. But unlike $CHRW , which had an average 3Q payroll about 10% less than a year ago, Expeditors isn't slashing bodies. pic.twitter.com/WAYt3VQNvb — John Kingston (@JohnHKingston) November 27, 2026
In line with that, Courtney Hawkins, the company’s CIO, said the “most important” slide she was showing to the audience was that Expeditors has had an 8.9% increase in shipments and a less than 1% drop in headcount. (The time frame for that point of comparison was not made clear).
By contrast, C.H. Robinson total headcount between the third quarter of 2025 and 2026 was down more than 10%.
At Bank of America Merrill Lynch, the team led by Ken Hoexter (who was on the investors’ day call) did not increase its rating on Expeditors, which already was at a Buy. But it increased its price target to $234 from $230.
Expeditors’ stock closed Friday at $199.46. It had closed November 18 at $188.88 and appears to have gotten some boost from the investors call, though given volatility in the overall market it can be challenging to cite the meeting as the cause of the increase.
The bank’s report also cited some of the data behind its improved price target. “Expeditors set a target for 5% to 7% long-term organic growth, and 12% to 15% EPS growth,” Bank of America Merrill Lynch said. “It raised its operating margin floor target (operating efficiency) to 32.5% from 30%.
Possible M&A reentry
Besides not holding earnings calls with analysts or investor days, one thing Expeditors also hasn’t done in a long time is make an acquisition.
Wall said Expeditors had not made a major acquisition since it entered the ocean business in 1986 with the acquisition of Pac Bridge. In recounting that, Wall noted he was a senior in high school that year.
But Hackett opened the door to that strategy changing.
In response to an analyst’s question, Hackett said an acquisition would need to be one that did not impact Expeditors’ culture, which the management team discussed at length earlier in the presentation.
But he added Expeditors had not been active in making acquisitions even when it was the type of deal that might not impact culture.
“We’re just going to be more active in the market to seize opportunities of value when they come up and provide competitive advantage,” Hackett said. But he added “I don’t want to go much further than that.”
Let’s do this again sometime
Toward the end of the call, Ravi Shanker of Morgan Stanley thanked the Expeditors’ management, adding that “I hope the message you guys are getting from us is we really like hearing from you, and we would like to hear from you more often.”
Shanker then got specific: any plans to add conference calls with analysts each quarter?
“We’re not committed yet,” Hackett said. “We’re evolving our investor relations strategy. This is part of that.”
To which Wall, who said earlier in the call that it was mostly Hackett who pushed the idea of the meeting, added, “Yes, this has been really uncomfortable.”
